reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
clinicalPearls: Aortic valve prolapse is displacement of one or more cusps into the left ventricular outflow tract during diastole, producing aortic regurgitation with an eccentric jet.

A key association is ventricular septal defect, where the right coronary or non-coronary cusp prolapses into a doubly committed subarterial or perimembranous defect, partially occluding the shunt while worsening regurgitation.
Progressive cusp prolapse is an indication to close a ventricular septal defect even when the shunt is small, to prevent worsening aortic regurgitation.
It is also seen with bicuspid valve, connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, and myxomatous degeneration.
Echocardiography shows diastolic cusp displacement below the annular plane with a regurgitant jet directed away from the prolapsing cusp.
The murmur is an early decrescendo diastolic murmur, and a cusp prolapsing over a ventricular septal defect may reduce the systolic shunt murmur over time.
Early valve-sparing repair is preferred before the cusp tissue becomes irreversibly elongated and damaged.
reference.pathophysiology: Prolapse occurs when a cusp loses adequate support and herniates below the plane of the aortic annulus into the left ventricular outflow tract during diastole, causing malcoaptation and regurgitation. A common mechanism is deficient subvalvar cusp support in ventricular septal defect, where loss of tissue beneath the cusp together with a Venturi effect from the high-velocity shunt draws the right coronary or non-coronary cusp into the defect; doubly committed subarterial and perimembranous defects are the typical culprits. Other causes include redundant myxomatous cusp tissue and connective tissue disease. Sustained prolapse leads to cusp elongation, fibrosis and progressively worsening aortic regurgitation with left ventricular volume overload.
additionalDifferentials: Aortic root dilatation causing central regurgitation
Subaortic membrane with secondary cusp damage
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography assessing cusp motion and the regurgitant jet
Transoesophageal and 3D echocardiography for cusp morphology
Cardiac MRI for regurgitant fraction and left ventricular volumes
Screening for ventricular septal defect and measurement of aortic root dimensions
redFlags: Severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular dilatation or dysfunction
Rapidly progressive prolapse over a ventricular septal defect
Fever, new murmur or emboli suggesting infective endocarditis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on early recognition and timely surgery; valve-sparing repair before significant cusp degeneration gives good results, whereas late presentation with severe regurgitation and left ventricular dysfunction worsens outcome.
pitfalls: Overlooking a small ventricular septal defect as the cause of progressive aortic regurgitation
Delaying ventricular septal defect closure until regurgitation is already severe
Misjudging jet severity on off-axis views of an eccentric prolapse jet
Attributing regurgitation to root dilatation when cusp prolapse is the primary lesion
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
management: Refer for aortic valve repair, favouring valve-sparing techniques, before significant cusp degeneration or left ventricular dysfunction develops
Close an associated ventricular septal defect, even when the shunt is small, once progressive cusp prolapse appears, to prevent worsening aortic regurgitation
Control blood pressure and afterload and treat any heart failure with diuretics and guideline-directed therapy while awaiting surgery
Address an underlying connective tissue disorder such as Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, slowing aortic root dilatation with a beta-blocker or ARB and monitoring root dimensions
Maintain good dental hygiene and endocarditis-prevention measures
Undertake serial echocardiographic surveillance of cusp motion, regurgitant severity and ventricular size, managing through a heart-valve multidisciplinary team
